ch39.note: In the civil war 'gray' marked ground—or a man—of divided, ambiguous allegiance, neither firmly Nationalist ('white') nor Communist ('red'). A 'gray figure' could pass between both sides, and the 'gray zones' were the contested country where neither writ fully ran.

'Peace-preservation' (保安, baoan) units were local security militia raised at county and district level for defense and policing, separate from the regular army—the home guard of the pacified areas, of uneven training and loyalty.

Until the twentieth century many Chinese women had their feet tightly bound from girlhood, leaving them small and deformed and their owners barely able to walk. That a bound-footed woman could rally the defenders on the stockade wall for three days and nights is the point of the wonder.
The 'Nine Springs' (九泉) is a classical name for the world of the dead deep underground; to 'close one's eyes at the Nine Springs' is to rest easy in death, one's cares on earth discharged.

In Chinese custom a proper burial coffined in the earth (rather than left exposed) mattered greatly to the peace of the dead. To provide a coffin for every fallen man—even the enemy's dead—was therefore a marked and costly act of mercy.

'Sons-and-brothers troops' (子弟兵, zidibing) are soldiers raised from a commander's own home region and bound to him by personal and native-place loyalty. Fu Zuoyi's favoring of his own such units over centrally assigned ones is the 'parochialism' Chen lays against him.
